items.title: I can distinguish between unicellular and multicellular organisms and describe the trade-offs of each
items.what: Unicellular organisms perform all life functions in a single cell, while multicellular organisms divide those functions among specialised cells. Being multicellular is more energy-efficient per function but requires greater organisational complexity.
items.why: This distinction explains why complex organisms need systems at all, and sets up the logic of specialisation and organisation throughout the chapter.
items.example: An amoeba absorbs nutrients, excretes waste and responds to stimuli all within one cell. A human assigns each of those roles to entire organ systems made of hundreds of cell types.

subtopic.name: From Cells to Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the hierarchy of biological organisation from specialised cells through tissues, organs, systems and organisms. Compares unicellular and multicellular organisation in animals and plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding this hierarchy is foundational to all of Unit 1 AOS2. It explains why multicellular organisms need transport and regulatory systems, and underpins every system studied in this chapter.

items.title: I can explain how the structure of a specialised animal cell relates to its function
items.what: Specialised cells have structural features that are directly adapted to their function, such as shape, organelle content or surface modifications. These adaptations maximise the efficiency of a single task.
items.why: Structure-function relationships are a recurring exam theme and connect cell biology to organ system physiology throughout the course.
items.example: A red blood cell has a biconcave disc shape, which maximises its surface area to volume ratio for oxygen diffusion across the plasma membrane, and it lacks a nucleus to maximise haemoglobin content.

subtopic.name: From Cells to Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the hierarchy of biological organisation from specialised cells through tissues, organs, systems and organisms. Compares unicellular and multicellular organisation in animals and plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding this hierarchy is foundational to all of Unit 1 AOS2. It explains why multicellular organisms need transport and regulatory systems, and underpins every system studied in this chapter.

items.title: I can define tissue, organ and biological system, and describe the relationship between these levels
items.what: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is formed when two or more tissue types act together; a system is a group of organs cooperating to perform a survival function. Each level builds on the one below.
items.why: These definitions are directly tested in VCE exams and provide the vocabulary needed to describe any body system accurately.
items.example: Cardiomyocytes form cardiac muscle tissue, which combines with connective, epithelial and nerve tissues to form the heart organ, which works with blood vessels and lungs as the circulatory system.

subtopic.name: From Cells to Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the hierarchy of biological organisation from specialised cells through tissues, organs, systems and organisms. Compares unicellular and multicellular organisation in animals and plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding this hierarchy is foundational to all of Unit 1 AOS2. It explains why multicellular organisms need transport and regulatory systems, and underpins every system studied in this chapter.

items.title: I can sequence the levels of cellular organisation from cell to organism and apply this to a specific example
items.what: The correct sequence is: specialised cell → tissue → organ → system → organism. This applies to both animals and plants and can be illustrated using any body system.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to trace this hierarchy using a named cell, and marks are awarded for including the function at each level.
items.example: Smooth muscle cell → smooth muscle tissue → bladder → urinary system → human. Each step up adds organisational complexity and a new emergent function.

subtopic.name: From Cells to Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the hierarchy of biological organisation from specialised cells through tissues, organs, systems and organisms. Compares unicellular and multicellular organisation in animals and plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding this hierarchy is foundational to all of Unit 1 AOS2. It explains why multicellular organisms need transport and regulatory systems, and underpins every system studied in this chapter.

items.title: I can explain why multicellular animals need transport systems, with reference to surface area to volume ratio
items.what: As organisms increase in size, their volume grows faster than their surface area, meaning diffusion alone cannot supply nutrients and remove waste fast enough. Transport systems overcome this limitation.
items.why: The SA:V ratio argument is a core quantitative concept in VCE Biology and directly justifies the existence of the digestive, circulatory and excretory systems.
items.example: A single-celled organism 10 µm across can rely on diffusion, but a human liver cell is micrometres from the nearest capillary precisely because the circulatory system has reduced effective diffusion distances.

subtopic.name: From Cells to Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the hierarchy of biological organisation from specialised cells through tissues, organs, systems and organisms. Compares unicellular and multicellular organisation in animals and plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding this hierarchy is foundational to all of Unit 1 AOS2. It explains why multicellular organisms need transport and regulatory systems, and underpins every system studied in this chapter.

items.title: I can identify the ten systems of the human body and state a key function of each
items.what: Mammals have ten interconnected body systems: nervous, respiratory, endocrine, immune, lymphatic, circulatory, urinary, digestive, musculoskeletal and reproductive. No system operates in complete isolation.
items.why: Knowing all ten systems and their interactions supports answers to extended-response questions that require cross-system examples.
items.example: The endocrine system releases ADH, which acts on the urinary system to increase water reabsorption in the nephron — a direct interaction between two named systems.

subtopic.what: Covers the hierarchy of biological organisation from specialised cells through tissues, organs, systems and organisms. Compares unicellular and multicellular organisation in animals and plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding this hierarchy is foundational to all of Unit 1 AOS2. It explains why multicellular organisms need transport and regulatory systems, and underpins every system studied in this chapter.

items.title: I can define the four processes of the digestive system: ingestion, digestion, absorption and egestion
items.what: Ingestion is food entering via the mouth; digestion is the physical and chemical breakdown of food; absorption is the movement of nutrients into the bloodstream; egestion is the removal of undigested waste via the anus.
items.why: These four terms define the overall role of the system and are frequently used as the framework for extended-response answers about digestion.
items.example: When you eat a sandwich, ingestion occurs at the mouth, digestion of starch begins there too, glucose is absorbed through villi in the jejunum, and cellulose fibre is egested as faeces.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can distinguish between physical and chemical digestion and give examples of each
items.what: Physical (mechanical) digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing surface area without changing chemical composition. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into absorbable subunits.
items.why: Understanding how these two processes complement each other is essential for explaining why chewing speeds up chemical digestion and for interpreting enzyme pH graphs in exam questions.
items.example: Teeth physically crush bread into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for salivary amylase to chemically break starch into maltose — the enzyme acts faster because more surface is accessible.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can describe the role of each organ and accessory organ along the gastrointestinal tract
items.what: The GI tract includes the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) and large intestine. Accessory organs — liver, gall bladder and pancreas — contribute digestive secretions but are not part of the tube itself.
items.why: Identifying structures and their functions is directly tested in short-answer questions, including diagram labelling tasks.
items.example: The pancreas secretes amylase, trypsin and lipase into the duodenum, along with bicarbonate to neutralise acidic chyme arriving from the stomach and restore a pH suitable for these enzymes.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can explain the role of the three major classes of digestive enzymes and their substrates and products
items.what: Amylases break polysaccharides (starch) into disaccharides then monosaccharides. Proteases (pepsin, trypsin, peptidases) break proteins into peptides then amino acids. Lipases break fats into glycerol and fatty acid chains.
items.why: Enzyme substrate-product relationships are regularly tested, including questions linking enzyme location to the pH conditions present in that organ.
items.example: Pepsin is active at pH 2–3 in the stomach and cleaves proteins into peptides; trypsin is active at pH 6–8 in the small intestine and continues protein breakdown — their different optimal pH values reflect their different locations.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can describe the specialised cells of the stomach and their individual roles
items.what: Four specialised cells line the stomach: goblet cells secrete mucus to protect the lining; parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid; chief cells secrete pepsin; G cells secrete the hormone gastrin, which stimulates acid production.
items.why: This is a specific study design requirement and demonstrates how multiple specialised cell types cooperate within a single organ.
items.example: Goblet cells are essential because without their mucus layer, the hydrochloric acid secreted by parietal cells would digest the stomach wall itself — a failure of this protection leads to gastric ulcers.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can explain how the structure of the small intestine maximises nutrient absorption
items.what: The small intestine is approximately 6 m long, highly folded, and lined with villi (0.5–1.6 mm fingerlike projections), each covered in microvilli (~1 µm). Together these features create a total absorptive surface area of approximately 250 m².
items.why: This is a direct application of the SA:V ratio principle and is a high-frequency exam topic, including questions that link villi structure to absorption mechanisms.
items.example: Without villi and microvilli, the internal surface of the small intestine would be roughly the size of a bath towel. With them, it is the size of a tennis court — a roughly 600-fold increase in absorptive area.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can explain how different nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine and by what method
items.what: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed into capillaries within villi by facilitated diffusion and active transport. Glycerol and fatty acids, being lipid-soluble, diffuse into lacteals (lymphatic vessels) within villi. Water is absorbed by osmosis.
items.why: Membrane transport mechanisms are linked directly to the digestive system in exam questions, requiring students to specify the method and direction for each nutrient.
items.example: Glucose moves from the jejunum lumen (high concentration after a meal) into the blood (lower concentration) via facilitated diffusion using carrier proteins, then travels via the portal vein to the liver.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can describe the cause and consequences of coeliac disease and heartburn
items.what: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition where gluten triggers immune attack on small intestine cells, flattening villi and reducing absorption. Heartburn results from a weakened cardiac sphincter allowing gastric acid into the oesophagus.
items.why: Malfunctions are explicitly required by the study design and test whether students can apply structural knowledge to explain physiological consequences.
items.example: In coeliac disease, flattened villi reduce the absorptive surface area of the small intestine, leading to nutrient deficiencies including iron deficiency anaemia and vitamin D deficiency causing bone weakness.

subtopic.name: The Digestive System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
subtopic.why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can define homeostasis and explain the general role of the endocrine system in maintaining it
items.what: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes in the external environment. The endocrine system achieves this by releasing hormones that travel in the blood to target cells and initiate corrective responses.
items.why: Homeostasis underpins the entire endocrine and excretory system content and is a recurring theme in Unit 3/4 Biology, particularly in feedback loop questions.
items.example: When blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which signals liver and muscle cells to take up and store glucose — returning blood glucose to the normal range of approximately 4–6 mmol/L.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can identify the major endocrine glands and the hormones they produce
items.what: Key glands include the hypothalamus, pituitary (anterior and posterior), pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas and gonads (testes and ovaries). Each gland secretes specific hormones with defined target tissues.
items.why: Gland-hormone-function relationships are directly tested in matching and short-answer questions and are the structural foundation for understanding malfunction conditions.
items.example: The pancreas contains islets of Langerhans with alpha cells secreting glucagon and beta cells secreting insulin — two antagonistic hormones that together regulate blood glucose concentration.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can describe the three-step process by which all hormones exert control on target cells
items.what: A specialised endocrine cell secretes a hormone into the bloodstream; the hormone travels to a target cell with a complementary receptor; binding to the receptor initiates a specific cellular response.
items.why: This three-step model applies to every hormone in the study design and is the basis for understanding why some cells respond to a hormone and others do not.
items.example: Insulin is secreted by beta cells, travels in the blood to liver cells, and binds to insulin receptors on the liver cell membrane — triggering uptake and conversion of glucose to glycogen.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can distinguish between protein-based and lipid-based hormones and explain how each type interacts with its target cell
items.what: Protein-based hormones are hydrophilic and cannot cross the plasma membrane, so they bind to surface receptors. Lipid-based hormones are hydrophobic and diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer to bind intracellular receptors.
items.why: This distinction is directly linked to membrane structure concepts and is tested in questions asking students to select or justify which receptor diagram applies to a named hormone.
items.example: Insulin (protein-based) binds to a receptor on the outer plasma membrane of liver cells. Testosterone (lipid-based) diffuses through the membrane and binds to a receptor in the cytosol, which then moves to the nucleus to affect gene expression.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can explain the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis in regulating other endocrine glands
items.what: The hypothalamus monitors internal conditions and releases hormones that stimulate or inhibit the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then releases tropic hormones (such as TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) that act on other endocrine glands.
items.why: This hierarchical control system is a key example of negative feedback and appears in extended-response questions requiring students to trace a hormone pathway from stimulus to response.
items.example: Low body temperature detected by the hypothalamus triggers TRH release, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH, which stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine, increasing metabolic rate and heat production.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can describe the specialised cells of the pancreas, thyroid, thymus and gonads and the hormones they produce
items.what: The pancreas contains alpha cells (glucagon) and beta cells (insulin) in the islets of Langerhans. The thyroid contains follicular cells (thyroxine) and parafollicular cells (calcitonin). The thymus contains epithelial cells releasing thymosin. The testes contain Leydig cells (testosterone) and the ovaries contain granulosa cells (oestrogen).
items.why: Specific cell types and their hormone products are study design requirements and appear in questions linking gland structure to hormone function.
items.example: Thymosin is released by epithelial cells in the thymus when immature T-cells arrive from bone marrow, causing the T-cells to mature into functional immune cells before entering the bloodstream.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can describe the cause and consequences of type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes and Graves' disease
items.what: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells, eliminating insulin production. Type 2 results from long-term insulin resistance, exhausting beta cells. Graves' disease is an autoimmune condition where antibodies mimic TSH, overstimulating the thyroid to produce excess thyroxine.
items.why: Endocrine malfunctions are required by the study design and test application of hormone mechanisms to pathological contexts.
items.example: In Graves' disease, abnormal antibodies bind to TSH receptors on the thyroid, continuously stimulating thyroxine production independent of the hypothalamus-pituitary feedback loop, resulting in a metabolic rate far above normal and symptoms including weight loss, increased heart rate and heat intolerance.

subtopic.name: The Endocrine System
subtopic.what: Covers the structure and function of the major endocrine glands, the mechanism of hormone action on target cells, the role of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, and the malfunctions of diabetes and Graves' disease.
subtopic.why: The endocrine system demonstrates chemical signalling and homeostasis, which are central themes in VCE Biology Units 1 and 3/4. It also provides concrete examples of protein-based versus lipid-based molecules and their membrane interactions.

items.title: I can explain the origin of nitrogenous waste and why it must be excreted
items.what: Excess amino acids cannot be stored and are broken down by deamination in the liver. This releases the amine group, which is converted to toxic ammonia and then to less toxic urea for excretion in urine.
items.why: Understanding why nitrogenous waste forms and why different organisms excrete different forms (ammonia, urea, uric acid) is a study design requirement that connects metabolism to excretion.
items.example: A fish living in water excretes ammonia directly across its gills because water is abundant. Humans convert ammonia to urea in the liver because urea is far less toxic and requires less water to excrete — an adaptation for terrestrial life.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can identify the structures of the mammalian excretory system and describe the role of each
items.what: The system includes two kidneys (filter blood), two ureters (carry urine to the bladder), the bladder (stores urine) and the urethra (expels urine). The renal artery delivers blood and the renal vein returns filtered blood.
items.why: Structural identification of excretory organs is directly tested and provides the spatial context needed to explain filtration and reabsorption processes.
items.example: Each kidney receives oxygenated blood via the renal artery, filters approximately 180 litres of plasma per day, and returns cleaned blood via the renal vein — only about 1.8 litres of urine is actually excreted.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can describe the nephron as the functional unit of the kidney and identify its key structural regions
items.what: The nephron consists of the Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle (descending and ascending), distal tubule and collecting duct. It is closely associated with the glomerulus and peritubular capillaries.
items.why: The nephron is the site of filtration, reabsorption and secretion and is the focus of the most complex excretory system exam questions, including those linking osmosis and active transport to specific tubule regions.
items.example: Each human kidney contains approximately 0.8–1.5 million nephrons. If all nephrons from both kidneys were laid end to end, the total tubule length would be approximately 80 km.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can explain filtration, reabsorption and secretion in the nephron and where each occurs
items.what: Filtration: blood pressure forces water and small solutes from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule (proteins are excluded). Reabsorption: useful substances and water move from the tubule back into peritubular capillaries. Secretion: additional waste solutes are actively transported from blood into the tubule.
items.why: These three processes define how the nephron converts blood plasma into urine and are the basis for all quantitative questions about changes in filtrate composition along the nephron.
items.example: By the end of the proximal tubule, 65% of filtered water and ions, and 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids, have been reabsorbed. By the collecting duct, 99% of filtrate has been reclaimed, leaving approximately 1.8 L of urine per day.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can trace the change in filtrate composition from the Bowman's capsule to the collecting duct
items.what: Filtrate in the Bowman's capsule contains water, glucose, amino acids, ions and urea (no proteins). As it progresses, glucose and amino acids are fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, water is continuously reabsorbed, and urea becomes increasingly concentrated, representing 2% of urine compared to 0.03% in blood plasma.
items.why: Tracing composition changes is a standard exam task and requires integrating knowledge of osmosis, active transport and ADH regulation in a single coherent sequence.
items.example: A patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes will have glucose present in their urine, because blood glucose is so elevated that the proximal tubule transport proteins become saturated and cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can explain the role of ADH in regulating water reabsorption and how this connects the excretory and endocrine systems
items.what: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is released from the posterior pituitary when blood osmolality rises (e.g. during dehydration). It increases the water permeability of the distal tubule and collecting duct, allowing more water to be reabsorbed by osmosis.
items.why: ADH action is a key cross-system example linking the endocrine and excretory systems, and it is a model for how negative feedback maintains water homeostasis.
items.example: After running 10 km without drinking, blood solute concentration rises above the normal range. The posterior pituitary releases more ADH, the collecting duct becomes more permeable to water, urine volume decreases and becomes more concentrated — often darker yellow in colour.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can describe the cause, symptoms and consequences of UTIs and kidney disease
items.what: UTIs are bacterial infections (typically E. coli) of the urethra or bladder, more common in females due to the shorter urethra (4 cm vs 20 cm in males). Chronic kidney disease involves progressive loss of nephron function and can require dialysis or transplant.
items.why: Excretory system malfunctions are study design requirements and test whether students can apply structural and functional knowledge to pathological contexts.
items.example: Chronic kidney disease can progress to 90% loss of nephron function before symptoms appear, because the remaining nephrons hypertrophy and compensate. Once symptoms such as high blood pressure and oedema emerge, significant irreversible damage has usually already occurred.

subtopic.name: The Excretory System
subtopic.what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
subtopic.why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can define vascular and non-vascular plants and explain how this classification relates to their size and habitat
items.what: Vascular plants have specialised conducting tissue (xylem and phloem) for transporting water and nutrients. Non-vascular plants lack this tissue, so they rely on osmosis and diffusion, restricting them to small sizes and moist environments.
items.why: This classification establishes the structural basis for all subsequent plant transport content and is directly tested in questions asking students to justify size differences between plant groups.
items.example: A moss (non-vascular) can grow only a few centimetres tall because water moves cell-to-cell by osmosis. A mountain ash (vascular) can reach 99.6 m because xylem transports water from roots to canopy over that entire distance.

subtopic.name: Plant Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the classification of vascular and non-vascular plants, the structure and function of root and shoot systems, specialised cells of the xylem, the mechanism of transpiration, and the factors affecting transpiration rate.
subtopic.why: Plant systems provide a non-animal context for the same organisational principles covered in the mammalian systems, and transpiration is an important model of passive transport driven by concentration gradients and physical properties of water.

items.title: I can describe the root system and shoot system of a vascular plant and the function of each organ within them
items.what: The root system (roots) absorbs water and minerals, anchors the plant and stores food. The shoot system (stems and leaves) supports the plant, transports substances and carries out photosynthesis.
items.why: Knowing the systems and their organs is the plant equivalent of knowing mammalian body systems and is required for full marks on questions comparing animal and plant organisation.
items.example: Secondary roots branch laterally from the primary root, greatly increasing total surface area for water absorption — analogous to the role of villi and microvilli in the mammalian small intestine.

subtopic.name: Plant Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the classification of vascular and non-vascular plants, the structure and function of root and shoot systems, specialised cells of the xylem, the mechanism of transpiration, and the factors affecting transpiration rate.
subtopic.why: Plant systems provide a non-animal context for the same organisational principles covered in the mammalian systems, and transpiration is an important model of passive transport driven by concentration gradients and physical properties of water.

items.title: I can explain how the structure of root hair cells is specialised for water and mineral uptake
items.what: Root hair cells are elongated thin projections from the root epidermis that extend between soil particles. Their shape maximises surface area for osmotic water uptake and active transport of mineral ions, without increasing the volume of the root.
items.why: Root hair cells are a named example in the study design of structure-function relationships in plant cells and are a direct parallel to intestinal epithelial cells in the mammalian digestive system.
items.example: A single rye plant has been estimated to have over 14 billion root hair cells with a combined surface area of approximately 400 m² — comparable to the absorptive surface of the human small intestine.

subtopic.name: Plant Systems
subtopic.what: Covers the classification of vascular and non-vascular plants, the structure and function of root and shoot systems, specialised cells of the xylem, the mechanism of transpiration, and the factors affecting transpiration rate.
subtopic.why: Plant systems provide a non-animal context for the same organisational principles covered in the mammalian systems, and transpiration is an important model of passive transport driven by concentration gradients and physical properties of water.

items.title: I can describe the composition, arrangement and role of xylem tissue in vascular transport
items.what: Xylem consists of two dead cell types — vessel elements (open-ended cylinders) and tracheids (tapered, overlapping cells) — both lignified for strength. They form continuous hollow tubes from root to leaf for unidirectional upward water transport.
items.why: Xylem structure is a named study design requirement and demonstrates how dead cells can still perform a vital structural and transport function.
items.example: In a cross-section of a woody stem, the rings visible to the naked eye are annual layers of xylem. Each ring represents one year's growth, and the wood itself is composed entirely of lignified xylem cell walls.

items.title: I can distinguish between vessel elements and tracheids in terms of structure and water movement
items.what: Vessel elements are wider, cylindrical and open at both ends, allowing unrestricted water flow. Tracheids are narrower, taper at both ends and overlap, with water moving laterally through pits between cells. Both are lignified and dead at maturity.
items.why: This distinction is a specific study design requirement and is tested in diagram interpretation questions comparing the two cell types.
items.example: Angiosperms (flowering plants) have both vessel elements and tracheids; gymnosperms (conifers) rely primarily on tracheids. The presence of vessel elements in angiosperms is associated with more efficient water transport at higher flow rates.

items.title: I can explain the cause and role of transpiration and how the cohesion-tension mechanism drives water movement through the xylem
items.what: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from leaves through open stomata. This creates a negative pressure (tension) in the xylem, pulling water upward. Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls maintain a continuous water column.
items.why: Transpiration is the primary mechanism of water transport in tall plants and is a key passive transport example — it requires no ATP from the plant yet moves water over 100 m vertically.
items.example: In a California redwood at 115 m, the tension generated by transpiration at the canopy is sufficient to pull a continuous water column from roots to leaves. Cohesion stops the column from breaking under this tension.

items.title: I can explain the role of stomata and guard cells in regulating transpiration
items.what: Stomata are pores bordered by two guard cells. When guard cells are turgid (water-filled), the stoma opens; when they are flaccid, it closes. Opening allows CO₂ entry for photosynthesis but also increases water loss by transpiration.
items.why: Guard cell function is a direct application of osmosis to plant physiology and illustrates the balance plants must maintain between photosynthesis and water conservation.
items.example: On a hot dry day, guard cells lose water to surrounding cells by osmosis, becoming flaccid and closing the stomata. This reduces transpiration water loss but simultaneously limits CO₂ uptake and slows photosynthesis.

items.title: I can explain how light intensity, temperature, wind and humidity affect the rate of transpiration
items.what: Transpiration rate increases with higher light intensity (stomata open wider), higher temperature (faster kinetic energy and evaporation), and greater wind speed (removes water vapour, steepening the concentration gradient). High humidity decreases transpiration by reducing the concentration gradient between leaf and air.
items.why: Environmental factors affecting transpiration are explicitly listed in the study design and are tested in experimental design and data interpretation questions.
items.example: A potted plant in a sealed transparent container will show little mass loss because the enclosed humid air reaches saturation and the concentration gradient between stomata and air falls to near zero, effectively halting transpiration.
